body_html:
Spanish holiday phrases go well beyond ¡Feliz Navidad! Holidays in Spanish-speaking families are long, loud and full of food, and each one comes with its own greetings, toasts and traditions. Whether you are spending Christmas Eve with your partner’s family in Mexico, celebrating Thanksgiving with Spanish-speaking relatives in the United States or joining a Día de Muertos altar, a few well-chosen phrases help you feel part of it.

Quick answer
  • Christmas: ¡Feliz Navidad! ¡Felices fiestas!
  • New Year: ¡Feliz Año Nuevo! ¡Próspero Año Nuevo!
  • Toast: ¡Salud! Brindo por la familia.
  • For any holiday: ¡Que la pasen muy bien!
{{toc}}

Spanish holiday phrases for Christmas

SpanishEnglish
¡Feliz Navidad!Merry Christmas!
¡Felices fiestas!Happy holidays!
¡Feliz Nochebuena!Happy Christmas Eve!
Te deseo una Navidad llena de paz.I wish you a Christmas full of peace.
¿Qué te trajo Santa?What did Santa bring you?
¿Dónde van a pasar la Navidad?Where are you spending Christmas?

In Mexico and much of Latin America, the big celebration is la Nochebuena, the night of December 24, with a late family dinner and gifts at midnight. December 25 is often a quiet day of leftovers. In Mexico, the season starts with las posadas, nine nights of parties from December 16, with songs, piñatas and ponche, a warm fruit punch.

New Year’s Eve and New Year

SpanishEnglish
¡Feliz Año Nuevo!Happy New Year!
¡Próspero Año Nuevo!Have a prosperous New Year!
¡Feliz año!Happy New Year! (short, at midnight)
Que este año te traiga mucha salud.May this year bring you good health.
¿Cuáles son tus propósitos?What are your resolutions?

At midnight on Nochevieja (New Year’s Eve), many families eat twelve grapes, one for each chime of the clock, making a wish with each. In Mexico, some people wear red or yellow underwear for love or money in the new year, or walk around the block with a suitcase if they hope to travel. Don’t be surprised if you are handed a cup of grapes at 11:59 p.m.

{{image:2}}

Toasts and table talk

  • ¡Salud! Cheers!
  • Quiero hacer un brindis. I’d like to make a toast.
  • Brindo por la familia y por los que no están. Here’s to family, and to those who aren’t with us.
  • ¡Qué rico huele! It smells so good!
  • Todo está delicioso. Everything is delicious.
  • Gracias por recibirnos. Thank you for having us.

Holiday dinners are a perfect time to compliment the cook; see {{link:how-to-compliment-food-in-spanish|how to compliment food in Spanish}} and {{link:family-dinner-spanish-phrases|Spanish phrases for family dinner}}.

Thanksgiving in Spanish

Thanksgiving is el Día de Acción de Gracias, and many Spanish-speaking families in the United States celebrate it with a mix of turkey and their own dishes: tamales, rice, mole. Useful phrases:

  • ¡Feliz Día de Acción de Gracias! Happy Thanksgiving!
  • Doy gracias por tenerlos a todos aquí. I’m thankful to have you all here.
  • ¿Qué traes para la cena? What are you bringing to dinner?
  • el pavo turkey, el puré de papa mashed potatoes, el relleno stuffing

For more ways to say thanks, see {{link:ways-to-say-thank-you-in-spanish|ways to say thank you in Spanish}}.

Día de Muertos, Reyes and other celebrations

  • Día de Muertos (November 1–2) honors loved ones who have died with altars, marigolds and pan de muerto. It is a celebration, not a sad day. A respectful phrase: Qué bonito altar. ¿A quién se lo dedicaron? (What a beautiful altar. Who did you dedicate it to?)
  • Día de Reyes (January 6) celebrates the Three Kings. Families share a rosca de Reyes, and whoever finds the little figure inside hosts a tamal party on February 2.
  • Semana Santa (Holy Week) is a major holiday in much of Latin America and Spain: ¡Felices vacaciones de Semana Santa!
  • Día de las Madres in Mexico is always May 10: ¡Feliz Día de las Madres!

Holiday cards and messages

For a card or a group chat, these lines work for almost anyone:

  • Les deseamos una Feliz Navidad y un próspero Año Nuevo. We wish you a Merry Christmas and a prosperous New Year.
  • Que estas fiestas estén llenas de amor y alegría. May these holidays be full of love and joy.
  • Con cariño, de nuestra familia para la suya. With love, from our family to yours.
  • ¡Un abrazo enorme y felices fiestas! A big hug and happy holidays!

Sign off with Con cariño (With love) or Un abrazo (Hugs) for family and friends.

{{image:3}}

Common mistakes

  • ¡Feliz Navidades! Either ¡Feliz Navidad! or ¡Felices Navidades!, which is common in Spain.
  • ¡Buen Año Nuevo! The set phrase is ¡Feliz Año Nuevo!
  • Treating Día de Muertos as Halloween. They are different holidays. Avoid costumes that mock the traditions.
  • Leaving early. Holiday dinners often run past midnight. Leaving at 10 p.m. can seem rushed; if you must, say Con permiso, ya me tengo que ir. ¡Gracias por todo!

The capitalization of holiday names follows its own rules in Spanish; see {{link:spanish-capitalization-rules|Spanish capitalization rules}}, and the Diccionario panhispánico de dudas for doubtful cases.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Spanish holiday phrases open the door to some of the warmest moments in a family’s year. Learn the greetings, raise a glass with ¡salud!, ask about the traditions, and say yes to the twelve grapes. For other moments that matter, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you say Happy Holidays in Spanish?
faq.a: ¡Felices fiestas! works for the whole season.
Christmas Eve, December 24. In Mexico and much of Latin America it is the main family celebration.

faq.q: How do you make a toast in Spanish?
faq.a: Raise your glass and say ¡Salud!, or Quiero hacer un brindis por… followed by who or what you are toasting.

faq.q: Is Día de Muertos the same as Halloween?
faq.a: No. It is a Mexican tradition honoring loved ones who have died, celebrated on November 1 and 2.

questions.q: The big family night in Mexico at Christmas is…
questions.explain: Families celebrate on the night of December 24.

questions.q: What do many families eat at midnight on New Year’s Eve?
questions.explain: One grape for each chime, with a wish for each.
Provecho is said to someone eating.
